CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches and newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a 52-year-old male referred for neurosurgical consultation regarding a pituitary mass discovered during workup for worsening headaches. He presented to his primary care provider, Dr. Henry Howard, on 3/1/21 with complaints of worsening headaches over the preceding few months. Patient denies prior history of headaches. Workup with brain MRI and serology revealed an incidental pituitary lesion. Headaches are located behind the eyes and described as a dull, nagging ache. Onset was gradual approximately three months ago, initially 3/10 in severity and progressively worsening to current 6/10 severity. Headaches tend to be worse in the morning and typically last a few hours; nothing ameliorates or exacerbates them. Patient tried acetaminophen without relief. Recently reports bumping into door frames, which patient attributes to the mass compressing the optic chiasm noted on imaging. Denies associated nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Reports eyes were checked in the fall but denies subjective vision changes or balance disturbances.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Negative for fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, syncope, or nausea.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable. No chronic medical conditions.

MEDICATIONS
None. Patient attempted acetaminophen for headache relief without efficacy and discontinued.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Unknown. Patient is adopted.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as a computer programmer. Married for 25 years. Recently purchased a home. Denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use. Never has used these substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Alert, oriented to time, place, and person. Affect appropriate, speech fluent.
Neurological: Cranial nerves grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity normal. Eye movements normal. Pupils equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision normal.

RESULTS
Laboratory studies from 3/3/21: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, and CRP all within normal limits. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH; all other results normal.

MRI brain with contrast from 3/4/21: Well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles normal in size. No other abnormalities noted. Imaging consistent with benign-appearing pituitary adenoma.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Pituitary adenoma with optic chiasmal compression causing bitemporal hemianopia and progressive headaches. Surgical intervention indicated. Plan for transsphenoidal approach, a minimally invasive procedure through the sphenoid sinus. Patient counseled on surgical risks including anesthesia complications (myocardial infarction, stroke, death), infection, need for further surgery, wound complications such as cerebrospinal fluid leak, seizure, stroke, permanent neurological deficits (weakness, numbness, speech difficulty), and death. Referral to ophthalmology for comprehensive eye examination and visual field testing prior to surgery to map peripheral vision and provide baseline for post-operative comparison. Pre-operative visual field test to be scheduled today or tomorrow. Surgical scheduling to be arranged expeditiously. Patient understands plan and agrees to proceed with surgical intervention. Instructed to call with any questions or concerns.
